title: From Two Michelin Stars to the Grocery Aisle: Gymkhana Fine Foods Lands at Whole Foods Nationwide
excerpt: The premium Indian food brand, born from one of London's most celebrated restaurants, raises $8.5 million and launches simmer sauces across the U.S.
body:
Walk into any Whole Foods Market in America today and you will find something that, until very recently, would have been unthinkable: simmer sauces developed by the chefs of a two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant, sitting on shelves alongside the Raos and the Stonewall Kitchens of the world.

Gymkhana Fine Foods, the consumer brand spun out of London's legendary Gymkhana restaurant, has officially arrived in the United States — launching exclusively at Whole Foods stores nationwide. The move is backed by an $8.5 million Series A funding round led by CAVU Consumer Partners, the investment firm co-founded by "Shark Tank" star Rohan Oza and hedge fund veteran Brett Thomas.

## Restaurant to Retail

The Gymkhana restaurant, opened in 2013 by siblings Jyotin, Karam, and Sunaina Sethi of JKS Restaurants, has long been one of London's most acclaimed Indian dining experiences. Named for the historic gymkhana clubs of colonial India — gathering places for the elite — the restaurant earned its second Michelin star in London and has since expanded to Las Vegas, where it became the first Indian restaurant on the Strip, opening at the Aria Resort & Casino.

Now, co-founder Gulrez Singh Arora and the JKS team are translating that kitchen's recipes into retail products. The U.S. lineup features simmer sauces — Butter Masala, Goan Coconut Curry, Korma, Tikka Masala, and Madras — alongside marinades including Classic Tandoori BBQ, Green Tikka, and Roasted Garlic & Chili. Each retails between $8 and $10 and promises a restaurant-quality meal in under 30 minutes.

"Gymkhana restaurant has proved that Indian cuisine belongs at the highest level of global dining," Arora said. "Now we're bringing that magic into every kitchen. This isn't just a product launch — it's the beginning of Indian food's premium moment in America."

## The Premium Gap

The move addresses a long-standing gap in the American grocery market. Italian, Thai, and Japanese cuisines have had premium retail brands for years — think Rao's marinara or Mae Ploy curry paste. Indian food, despite accounting for more than $5 billion in at-home consumption across the U.S. and U.K., has historically lacked a restaurant-credentialed, premium-positioned offering at retail.

The gap is not for lack of demand. Indian food is now the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America, according to Dataessential. The U.S. ethnic food market is estimated at $24.5 billion. And the growth of the Indian diaspora — now exceeding 4.4 million — has created a consumer base that demands authenticity alongside convenience.

Gymkhana Fine Foods first launched in the U.K. in 2023, expanding to over 1,000 retail doors across Whole Foods Market UK, Waitrose, and Sainsbury's. According to Nielsen data, it has become the primary growth driver across total ambient sauce brands in the U.K. over the past 26 weeks, outpacing household names like Heinz and Mutti.

## Part of a Larger Wave

Gymkhana Fine Foods is hardly alone in recognizing the opportunity. Earlier this year, Chicago-based online marketplace Quicklly launched its "Just by Quicklly" ready-to-heat Indian meals at Costco and Aldi stores nationwide. ADF Foods' Truly Indian brand, which earned two NEXTY Award finalist placements at Natural Products Expo West in 2026, has expanded to over 1,300 stores with its line of frozen samosas, naans, and shelf-stable meals.

The trajectory mirrors what happened with Japanese cuisine a decade ago: a proliferation of restaurant openings, followed by premium CPG brands, followed by mainstream grocery penetration. The key difference is scale. India's culinary diversity — encompassing dozens of distinct regional traditions — means the runway for new product categories is enormous.

## What It Means for NRIs

For Indian Americans, the arrival of Gymkhana sauces at Whole Foods represents a cultural validation that goes beyond commerce. For decades, cooking Indian food at home in America meant sourcing spices from specialty stores and spending hours on preparation. The premium-brand approach does not replace that tradition — but it offers an alternative for busy weeknights that does not compromise on quality or authenticity.

"When I see Gymkhana on the shelf at my local Whole Foods, I feel something," one Indian-American food writer posted on social media. "It says: our food is not niche. It's not a curiosity. It belongs here."

Whether Gymkhana Fine Foods can replicate its U.K. success in the larger, more competitive American market remains the central question. But with CAVU's backing, Whole Foods' distribution muscle, and the broader tailwind of Indian cuisine's ascendance, the odds are better than they have ever been.

nri_angle: Gymkhana Fine Foods signals that Indian cuisine is finally getting the premium grocery treatment that Italian, Thai, and Japanese food achieved years ago — a milestone for diaspora food culture.
